newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Foreign workers replace Palestinians in Israel, report.
newsitem.headline: Foreign workers replace Palestinians in Israel, report.

text.p: Foreigners have replaced most of the Palestinians that once made up a major portion of Israel's workforce, a report by the Central Bureau of Statistics released on Wednesday showed.

Israel, which scaled down its Palestinian workforce because of security fears, is currently trying to boost the number of Palestinians working within its borders to relieve the Palestinian economy severely strained by the measure.
The bureau said Palestinian workers made only 0.7 percent of Israel's total labour force in April-June 1996, down from 2.2 percent in January-March 1994.
Foreign workers meanwhile grew to 3.8 percent of the labour force from 1.1 percent.

In Israel's agricultural and building sectors foreigners accounted for a quarter of the total workforce, up from 5.5-7.5 percent in first quarter of 1994. The number of Palestinians, who had once accounted for about 15 percent of the total, fell to 3.0-5.0 percent.
All told, foreigners and Palestinians comprised 4.5 percent of Israel's labour force in second quarter of 1996, up from 3.3 percent in first quarter of 1994.
The figures for non-Palestinian foreign workers are based on those reporting to the social security authority and therefore understate the actual number of such workers.

The bureau said that as of June 1996 some 81,000 foreign workers -- excluding Palestinians -- were registered with Israel's social security authority. It did not give figures for Palestinians working in Israel.
A bureau spokesman estimated the total number of foreign workers including those working illegally was 140,000.
The Palestinian Authority's Ministry of Employment says that currently 46,000 Palestinians from the West Bank and Gaza Strip work in Israel -- less than the 65,000 Israel says are allowed to enter.

Israeli and PLO officials say Israeli employers prefer foreign workers because Palestinians are subject to Israeli entry bans, normally imposed after attacks by Palestinian guerrillas or when such attacks are feared.
The Palestinian Monetary Authority recently put unemployment at around 60 percent in Gaza and 38 percent in the West Bank.
Israeli officials say they aim to gradually reduce the number of Asians and Eastern Europeans working in Israel and increase the number of permits to Palestinians over four years.
Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) have signed a series of interim peace deals since September 1993 setting up Palestinian self-rule enclaves in the West Bank and Gaza.
